slides.title: Articulatory phonetics + IPA
slides.body:
**Phonetics** = physical sounds of speech. **Phonology** = abstract sound system of a language.

**Articulatory phonetics** describes sounds by how they're produced:
• **Place of articulation**: where in vocal tract (bilabial, labiodental, dental, alveolar, post-alveolar, retroflex, palatal, velar, uvular, pharyngeal, glottal).
• **Manner of articulation**: how (stop/plosive, fricative, affricate, nasal, lateral, approximant, trill, tap).
• **Voicing**: voiced (vocal-fold vibration) or voiceless.
• **Vowels**: open-close (jaw position), front-back (tongue), rounded-unrounded (lips).

**International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA, 1888+)**: standard symbols for transcribing speech sounds across all languages.
- Pulmonic consonants: ~52 main symbols on the chart.
- Vowels: 28 cardinal positions (front/back × close/open × rounded/unrounded).
- Non-pulmonic: clicks (Khoisan), implosives, ejectives.
- Suprasegmentals: tone, stress, length, intonation.

Why IPA: language-independent + universally trained. Replaces orthography (English 'ough' has ~7 different pronunciations).

**Acoustic phonetics** measures speech waveforms:
- **Spectrogram**: time × frequency × intensity. Reveals formants, fricatives, stops, vowels.
- **Formants F1, F2, F3**: vocal-tract resonances. F1+F2 distinguish vowels (see viz).
- **VOT (voice onset time)**: gap between consonant release + voicing onset. /pa/ vs /ba/.
- **Pitch (F0)**: fundamental frequency. ~120 Hz adult male, ~210 Hz adult female. Tone-bearing in Mandarin etc.
- **Praat** + open-source tools enable acoustic analysis at PhD-or-undergraduate level.

slides.title: Phonemes vs allophones + phonological rules
slides.body:
**Phoneme**: abstract sound category that distinguishes meaning. Cross-linguistic differences:
- English /p/ vs /b/: distinct phonemes (pat vs bat).
- Korean /p/, /pʰ/, /p'/: 3 distinct phonemes (aspirated, unaspirated, tense).
- Mandarin /p/ + /pʰ/: distinct (ba vs pa); Mandarin lacks /b/.

**Allophone**: variant of a phoneme; predictable from context; doesn't distinguish meaning.
- English /p/ → [pʰ] word-initial (pat); [p] elsewhere (spat). Same phoneme, different allophones.
- Spanish /b/ → [b] after pause/nasal; [β] (fricative) intervocalically.

Discovering phonemes: **minimal pairs** (sip vs zip). If two sounds distinguish meaning, they're separate phonemes.

**Phonological rules** (generative tradition):
- /t/ → [tʰ] / # _ V (word-initial aspiration)
- /t/ → [ɾ] / V _ V (intervocalic flap in American English: 'butter' → 'budder')
- /n/ → [m] / _ p, b (assimilation: 'in possible' → 'impossible')
- Devoicing: /b/ → [p] word-finally (German: Tag /tak/)

**Phonological processes**:
- **Assimilation**: sounds become more like neighbors.
- **Dissimilation**: become less similar.
- **Deletion**: drop a sound (English 'going' → 'goin').
- **Insertion / epenthesis**: add a sound (Sp 'español' from L 'spanus').
- **Metathesis**: reorder (animal — animul).

**Optimality Theory (OT)** (Prince + Smolensky 1993): phonology as ranked constraints (faithfulness vs markedness). Modern dominant framework.

**Suprasegmental phonology**:
- **Tone**: lexical pitch contrast. Mandarin 4 tones; Cantonese 6-9.
- **Stress**: prominence on syllable. English (lexical stress); Czech (initial fixed).
- **Intonation**: utterance-level pitch contour. Distinguish statement / question / exclamation.

slides.title: Speech acoustics + perception
slides.body:
**Source-filter model** of speech production (Fant 1960):
- **Source**: vocal-fold vibration (voiced) or noise (voiceless fricative).
- **Filter**: vocal-tract resonances → spectral shaping.
- Vowels: source = periodic voicing; filter = formants F1, F2, F3.
- Fricatives: source = turbulent noise at constriction; filter = spectral peaks.
- Stops: silence (closure) + burst (release).

**Formant locations + meaning**:
- F1 (~300-800 Hz): inversely correlates with vowel height (jaw opening). /i, u/ have low F1; /a/ high F1.
- F2 (~800-2500 Hz): correlates with backness. /i/ has high F2; /u/ low F2.
- F3 (~2500-3500 Hz): rhoticity (R-coloring); some lip rounding.
- Speaker-normalization needed: women + children have higher formants (shorter vocal tract).

**Speech perception**:
- **Categorical perception**: continuous acoustic variation perceived in discrete categories. /pa-ba/ VOT continuum: sharp categorical boundary at ~30 ms.
- **Acoustic invariance vs context**: same phoneme has different acoustic realizations in different contexts (coarticulation); listeners normalize.
- **McGurk effect**: lip movement + audio integrate; /ba/ + visual /ga/ = perceived /da/.
- **Categorical learning**: infants learn language-specific categories ~6-12 months.

**Speech in technology**:
- **ASR (automatic speech recognition)**: HMM-GMM → DNN → end-to-end transformer (Whisper). Open-source: Wav2Vec, Whisper-Large; closed-source: Google, Amazon, Apple. Word-error rate <5% for many languages.
- **TTS (text-to-speech)**: concatenative → parametric → neural (Tacotron, FastSpeech, VALL-E, ElevenLabs). Near-human quality.
- **Speaker recognition**: identification + verification. Used in banking, security.
- **Forensic phonetics**: voice analysis for legal purposes.

question.question: Identify phoneme vs allophone via minimal pairs
question.goal: In English, do [p] (unaspirated) + [pʰ] (aspirated) represent separate phonemes or allophones of one phoneme?

steps.prompt: Can you find a minimal pair where [p] vs [pʰ] distinguishes meaning?
steps.reveal: No minimal pair: 'pat' [pʰæt] and 'spat' [spæt] — [pʰ] occurs word-initially, [p] after /s/. Switching them ('[pæt]' for 'pat') sounds odd but doesn't change meaning. Therefore allophones of a single phoneme.

[pʰ] occurs in stressed-syllable onsets: 'pat' [pʰæt]. [p] elsewhere, including post-/s/ clusters ('spat' [spæt]), unstressed positions, syllable codas ('cap' [kʰæp̚]). Predictable from environment → allophonic.

steps.prompt: How would the phonological rule be written?
steps.reveal: **Rule**: /p/ → [pʰ] / σ̂_onset _ V[+stress], where σ̂ marks stressed syllable. In other contexts /p/ → [p]. Cf. /t/ same rule + /k/ same. All voiceless stops aspirate in stressed-onset position.

steps.prompt: How would this work in Korean?
steps.reveal: Korean: 3 separate phonemes — plain /p/, aspirated /pʰ/, tense /p'/. Minimal triple: 불 /pul/ 'fire', 풀 /pʰul/ 'grass', 뿔 /p'ul/ 'horn'. Same English allophonic distinction is phonemic in Korean. Cross-linguistic differences in what's phonemic vs allophonic is foundational to phonology — same acoustic categories partitioned differently.

question.question: Order these phonological processes by frequency cross-linguistically (most common to least common).
question.explanation:
Cross-linguistic frequency of phonological processes:
• **Assimilation**: extremely common; near-universal. Nasal place assimilation, voicing assimilation, vowel harmony. Drives most cross-language alternations.
• **Deletion**: common, especially in casual speech + diachronic change. English 'going to' → 'gonna'.
• **Epenthesis**: moderately common. Languages with restricted syllable structure use it to repair illicit clusters (Sp 'spanish' → 'español').
• **Metathesis**: less common but well-attested. English 'animal' → 'animul'; OE 'brid' → 'bird'.
• **Spontaneous ejective creation**: rare. Ejectives are typologically uncommon (Caucasian languages, some African + American + Bering); usually emerge from sound-change involving glottal stop + obstruent.

The hierarchy reflects: assimilation is articulatorily-driven + universal; complex processes (metathesis, ejective creation) require specific historical contingencies. Naturalness-of-process is a major topic in phonological theory + Optimality-Theory constraint ranking.

question.question: Why do native speakers of one language often have difficulty perceiving distinctions in another language?
options: **Categorical perception**: by ~6-12 months, infants learn the phonemic categories of their native language; sounds that aren't contrastive in L1 are perceived as variants of a single category. Adult learners may struggle with: Japanese /r/ vs /l/ (single phoneme in Japanese); Mandarin tones (English-speakers); Hindi retroflex /ʈ/ vs dental /t̪/ (English /t/); /θ/ vs /s/ (many languages collapse). Perceptual training + experience can refine over months/years; perfect L2 phonology is rare after critical period (~10-12 yr).
question.explanation:
**Categorical perception + L1/L2 phonology**:

*Categorical perception phenomenon* (Liberman + colleagues 1957+):
- Adults perceive speech categorically: continuous acoustic variation (e.g., VOT) classified as discrete categories.
- Categories defined by L1 phoneme inventory.
- Hearing /pa/ vs /ba/: sharp boundary at VOT ~30 ms in English.

*Infant development*:
- 0-6 months: infants discriminate ALL phonemes universally.
- 6-12 months: 'perceptual narrowing' — infants lose sensitivity to non-native contrasts.
- 1+ year: L1 categorical perception established.

*Famous L2 difficulties*:

1. **Japanese /r/ vs /l/**: 
  - Japanese has single liquid /ɾ/ (alveolar tap).
  - English /r/ + /l/ distinction not contrastive in Japanese.
  - Japanese learners of English struggle: 'right' + 'light' sound the same to them.
  - Training studies (Lively + Pisoni 1993): high-variability phonetic training improves discrimination.

2. **Mandarin tones for English speakers**:
  - Mandarin has 4 tones + neutral; tone is phonemic (mā = mother, má = hemp, mǎ = horse, mà = scold).
  - English uses pitch for intonation (utterance-level), not lexically.
  - English speakers initially hear 'same word'; learn to discriminate over months-years.

3. **Hindi/Korean retroflex /ʈ/ vs dental /t̪/**:
  - English single /t/.
  - L2 speakers don't distinguish without training.

4. **Spanish/Italian /r/ vs /rr/** (tap vs trill):
  - English R is different; either may sound foreign.

5. **Click consonants (Khoisan)**:
  - !Xóõ has ~83 click phonemes.
  - Outsiders perceive them as a single category 'click.'

*Critical-period hypothesis* (Lenneberg 1967):
- Period (~puberty, ~10-12 yr) after which L2 acquisition particularly L2 phonology is harder.
- Not all-or-nothing: some adult learners achieve near-native phonology with effort + training; many don't.
- Phonology is the hardest aspect of L2; grammar + vocabulary continue to be learnable through adulthood.

*Plasticity + training*:
- High-variability phonetic training (HVPT): exposure to many speakers + contexts.
- Adaptive computer-based training (Pisoni et al.; modern: ELSA Speak).
- Some success with intense + targeted programs.
- Bilinguals (early + balanced) achieve near-native L2 phonology.

*Modern frontiers*:
- **Neural models**: do deep ASR systems show similar categorical perception?
- **Cross-linguistic phonemic universals**: which contrasts are easier/harder?
- **Adult plasticity**: limits + training optimization.
- **Music-language connections**: musicians sometimes have better tone perception.

Applications: L2 teaching; speech-recognition adaptation; voice-cloning (TTS in specific accents); accent reduction (controversial); forensic phonetics.

This is a beautiful case of cognitive constraints shaping behavior + culture.

hints: When do infants narrow their phonemic categories?
slides.workedSolution: Categorical perception: L1 phonemes learned in infancy ~6-12 months; sounds not contrastive in L1 perceived as same category. L2 difficulties: Japanese /r/ vs /l/, Mandarin tones, Hindi retroflex, Spanish trill. Critical period (~10-12 yr): adult L2 phonology hardest. Plasticity exists with training (HVPT, computer-adaptive). Modern: deep ASR shows similar patterns; cross-linguistic universals; neural+cognitive science studies.

question.question: Vowel /i/ formants: F1=270 Hz, F2=2290 Hz. F2/F1 ratio?
question.hint: 2290 / 270 ≈ 8.48. High F2/F1 ratio characterizes front close vowels like /i/.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why speech recognition + synthesis benefits from understanding phonetics + phonology.
question.rubric: Mentions: ASR + TTS systems benefit from understanding the structure of speech. Phonetic knowledge: acoustic features (formants, VOT, fricative spectral patterns); coarticulation effects; allophone variants. Phonological knowledge: phoneme inventories + permitted sequences + alternations + stress + intonation. Foundation of modern systems: phoneme-based acoustic models (HMM-GMM in 1990s-2010s; deep + transformer-based today). End-to-end neural systems (Whisper, Wav2Vec) increasingly learn phonetic + phonological structure implicitly from data, but supplementing with linguistic priors improves: low-resource languages, code-switching, accent variation, prosody-aware synthesis. TTS quality: high-quality outputs require phonological alignment (lexical stress, sandhi rules, intonation patterns). Languages without large training data benefit most from phonological priors. Concludes: linguistic knowledge + neural methods + data are complementary; modern speech engineering combines all three.
